## What

Acceptances, legal acceptance, organization setup and self-registrations have never reached the outbox in any release since v0.5.0, so hosts never received them (Closes #72).

The four outbox-forwarding reactors were pinned to the event log with `[EventLog]`. Chronicle's .NET client treats any type carrying an `EventSequenceAttribute` as a model-bound projection too (`ModelBoundProjectionsExtensions.IsModelBoundProjectionAttribute`, v19.4.7 and current main; upstream Cratis/Chronicle#4310). It registered an empty projection under each reactor's id, which took the observer over, so the reactors never received an event. No error was logged.

- Pin the reactors with `[Reactor(eventSequence: EventSequenceId.LogId)]`, which keeps them on the event log without projection discovery. Reactor ids are unchanged.
- Add a spec that fails if a forwarding reactor is discovered as a model-bound projection again.
- Resolve the scoped `IMongoCollection<AcceptedInvitation>` from a scope at startup and in the MongoDB health probe (it was captured from the root provider).
- Document the upgrade: affected releases, a second restart, and the republished backlog.

They then publish every historical acceptance, legal acceptance and registration from the start of the log. Hosts must consume these idempotently and decide how to treat old acceptances. Cratis/Direct#1319's granting is idempotent.

The two-argument constructor and two-value `Deconstruct` from Contracts 0.9.0 remain callable (with the original PascalCase parameter names, so named arguments still compile) but are now `[Obsolete]` and use the sentinel; the three-argument constructor / deconstruction carry expiry. ## Host upgrade

1. Mint a new canonical GUID for each invitation, including after revocation or acceptance. Append invitation/revocation facts under that event source ID in the host outbox.
2. Upgrade `Cratis.Ante.Contracts` and subscribe to both `InvitationTokenIssued` and the new `InvitationRejected` contract from Ante's outbox. Handle both rejection reasons. Ignore any rejection delivered after a host ID is already closed, and deduplicate `InvitationRejected` and `InvitationTokenIssued` per invitation id and event type: replay/redelivery can republish them and issue a new token, which should replace the one you hold rather than trigger another message.
3. Consume generation-2 `InvitationTokenIssued.ExpiresAt` as the UTC JWT expiry. Do not send a link or extend validity if expiry is `UnixEpoch` (unknown). Existing generation-1 contract mirrors must tolerate the new `expiresAt` JSON member. Rebuild callers to pass an actual expiry and use three-value deconstruction where applicable; the old CLR signatures remain available but are obsolete.
4. Verify host observer registration, namespace/routing, and idempotent consumption before deployment. See `Documentation/host-integration.md` and `Documentation/contracts.md`.

## Summary

This is the second work package of the onboarding-security epic (#10), building on the expiring/retry-safe invitation exchange from #12. It adds the authorization gate itself: `ISignedInIdentity.IsVerifiedOwnerOf(InvitationId)` verifies that the caller either presents the invite token's own `jti` claim for the invitation, or has a live, unexpired `AcceptedInvitation` session recorded under their own subject for that exact invitation. Both invitation-bound commands (`AcceptInvitation`, `SetupOrganization`) gate on it through their `CommandValidator`, so a mismatched or missing owner is rejected before `Handle()` ever runs and no event is appended.

`RegisterOrganization` (self-service registration, with no invitation to own) is unchanged - it has no invitation target to verify ownership against. The issue's broader acceptance criteria around read-side exposure (status/pending-list/identity queries keyed only by invitation id) and a redesigned owner-bound registration operation are follow-on work, not addressed here.

With Arc's MongoDB integration and Chronicle together, a projected read model now lands in the collection Arc reads. For example, `Author` is written to `Authors`. Before this, Chronicle's JVM client named the container after the read model's identifier, which is not pluralized, and apps needed a `NamingPolicy` bean with `pluralizeReadModelNames = false` as a workaround.

## Added

- An `arcReadModelNamingPolicy` bean that adapts Arc's `NamingPolicy` into Chronicle's `ReadModelNamingPolicy`; Chronicle's starter hands it to the `ChronicleOptions` it builds. It names the container only; the read model identifier is unchanged.
- The bean is registered only when exactly one Arc `NamingPolicy` exists and the application has not declared its own `ReadModelNamingPolicy`; an application policy wins. The auto-configuration now runs after the MongoDB one, so it sees Arc's default policy.

## Changed

- Updated to Chronicle.Kotlin 6.10.0, which adds `ReadModelNamingPolicy` (Cratis/Chronicle.Kotlin#105).
- Apps on Arc's default Mongo policy now get the pluralized collection Arc was already reading. Apps using `pluralizeReadModelNames = false` get identical names, so the workaround can be removed.
- Upgrade action: the kernel keeps the new container name but does not replay the projection for a container-only change, and the previous, unread collection is not deleted. Replay affected projections after upgrading and drop the old collection yourself. A running kernel may keep writing to the old container until its projection pipeline is rebuilt, for example on restart.
- The camel-casing setup snippets (Kotlin and Java) no longer include the workaround. The read-model naming documentation explains how the policy reaches Chronicle, the override, the case without Arc's policy, and the own-`ChronicleOptions` case, where the app calls `withReadModelNamingPolicy` itself (Cratis/Documentation#19).

Materialized read-model paging in the Kotlin client sent a 1-based page (`skip / take + 1`), but the kernel counts pages from 0. So `getInstances(X, 0, 50)` asked for page 1, and a first page was empty whenever the read model had no more than `take` instances. `observeInstances` had the same bug.

- `ReadModelsJavaBridge` delegates to this class, so Java callers get the fix too.
- No public API change; `apiCheck` passes.

## Defect

`ConcurrencyScope` in the JVM SDK was missing support for the `ExpectsNoMatchingEvent` field declared as field 7 in the `sequences.proto` contract:

```protobuf
message ConcurrencyScope {
   uint64 SequenceNumber = 1;
   bool EventSourceId = 2;
   string EventStreamType = 3;
   string EventStreamId = 4;
   string EventSourceType = 5;
   repeated EventType EventTypes = 6;
   bool ExpectsNoMatchingEvent = 7;   // ← was never settable from JVM
}
```

The SDK had no property, no builder method, and no mapping for this field. A JVM caller had no way to express _"append only if no matching event exists"_, making safe aggregate creation (idempotent first-event guards) impossible.

Tracked as #78. Unblocks Arc.Kotlin #176.

## Wire semantics

`ExpectsNoMatchingEvent = true` tells the kernel to reject the append if _any_ event matching the narrowed scope already exists. The narrowing dimensions (event source id, stream type, stream id, source type, event types) work exactly as they do for sequence-number-based checks — they can be combined to restrict the scope of the "no event" assertion.

**Contradictory combination rejected:** setting this flag together with a concrete expected `sequenceNumber` is a programming error. A concrete sequence number implies events exist (the history is at a known position), while `expectsNoMatchingEvent` implies no event exists. Sending both would produce an ambiguous request. The SDK now enforces this with an `init` block `require` on `ConcurrencyScope` so the error is caught at construction time regardless of how the object is built:

```
require(!(expectsNoMatchingEvent && sequenceNumber.isActualValue)) {
    "expectsNoMatchingEvent and a concrete sequenceNumber are mutually exclusive"
}
```

`isIncomplete` was also updated: a scope that carries only the flag (no concrete sequence number) is _not_ incomplete — the kernel has a well-defined check to perform without one.

## Added

- `IEventStore.registerAll()` registers every artifact in one call, and `awaitRegistration()` waits for the automatic pass so the first append is deterministic.
- `ChronicleOptions.withoutAutoRegistration()` turns discovery off, and `withArtifactsFrom(vararg packages)` narrows it to the packages you own. `KnownClientArtifacts` takes an explicit list where classpath scanning is unwanted.
- `IArtifactActivator` lets a dependency injection container create artifacts, so a reactor or reducer can take its dependencies through its constructor.
- Reactor, reducer and read model reactor handlers may be `suspend`, so a handler that awaits an HTTP call or the event log no longer blocks the thread the observation runs on. (#16)
- `IReactorMiddleware` wraps every reactor handler invocation, keeping tracing, logging and metrics out of reactor code. Java implements `BlockingReactorMiddleware` instead. (#11)
- A reactor handler may take parameters beyond the event — a read model resolved for the event's event source out of the box, or anything an `IReactorMethodArgumentResolver` supplies. (#27)
- `ICanBeNotifiedAboutReplay` tells a reactor when a replay begins and ends, per partition. (#13)
- `store.failedPartitions` surfaces the partitions an observer is stuck on, with the history of attempts, and retries one once the cause is fixed. (#13)
- `ConceptAs<T>` gives a domain value a type of its own, so the compiler can tell a book's identifier from a member's. Concepts serialize as the value they wrap, so adopting one for a property already in production changes neither the JSON nor the schema. (#15)
- `AppendOptions.causation` and `EventForEventSourceId.causation` attribute an append to a chain other than the ambient one — an imported event, or a side effect that belongs to a chain of its own. (#43)
- Chronicle work is reported as OpenTelemetry spans: appends, batches, reactor observations and reducer folds. Nothing to turn on. (#18)
- `IProjectionsService.query(declaration)` runs a Projection Declaration Language declaration and returns what it projected, without registering anything. (#19)

## Summary

Brings the Kotlin/Java Chronicle client to parity with the other Chronicle clients across two phases of work:

1. **Earlier phase**: four new service modules (ExternalServices, Webhooks, Jobs, EventStoreSubscriptions), event type migrations, 15 new model-bound projection attributes, a richer declarative projection builder, a richer ReadModels API, reactor side-effect events, and PII encryption key deletion.
2. **This phase**: three confirmed bug fixes, full `IEventSequence`/`IEventLog` completeness (redact, concurrency scopes, bookmarked reads, stream completion, a live append feed), `IEventStore` interface completeness, a richer `UnitOfWork`, constraint scoping, and typed read-model observation.

Fully additive — nothing existing changes behavior, except one safe, pre-release-only behavior change noted below.

## Added

### Service modules, migrations, projections, read models (earlier phase)

- `ExternalServices` — register named HTTP or database (MS SQL / PostgreSQL) endpoints with basic/bearer/OAuth authentication, addressable by name from other Chronicle integrations.
- `Webhooks` — register webhooks either via a discoverable `@Webhook` + `IWebhookDefiner` class or imperatively, with authentication, header, event-type filtering, and replay/activation options; list and remove webhooks.
- `Jobs` — list jobs and their steps, get a single job, and stop/resume/delete a job.
- `EventStoreSubscriptions` — subscribe an event store to another event store's outbox with optional event-type filtering, list, and unsubscribe. Now defaults to every event type this client has registered when a subscription isn't narrowed explicitly, instead of subscribing to nothing.
- Event type migrations — `IEventTypeMigration`/`EventTypeMigration` base class plus an `EventTypeMigrationBuilder` DSL (`renamedFrom`, `defaultValue`, `split`, `combine`) for upcasting/downcasting between event type generations, discovered alongside `@EventType` classes at `register()`.
- 15 new model-bound projection attributes: `@Join`, `@ChildrenFrom`, `@Nested`, `@ClearWith`, `@Count`, `@Increment`, `@Decrement`, `@AddFrom`, `@SubtractFrom`, `@FromAll`, `@FromEvery`, `@NotRewindable`, `@RemovedWith`, `@RemovedWithJoin`, `@NoAutoMap`.
- Declarative projection builder methods: `.join()`, `.fromEvery()`/`.fromAll()`, `.removedWith()`/`.removedWithJoin()`, `.children()`, `.nested()`, `.notRewindable()`, plus composite/constant keys.
- Reactor handlers can now return a follow-up event, a `List<Any>`, or the new `EventForEventSourceId` wrapper, and it's auto-appended as a side effect — same-stream or cross-stream.
- `ComplianceService.deleteEncryptionKey` for permanently erasing a subject's PII ("right to be forgotten").

### `IEventSequence` / `IEventLog` completeness (this phase)

- **`redact` / `redactForEventSource`** — permanently rewrites one event's content, or every event's content for an event source (optionally narrowed to specific event types). Destructive and irreversible; the single most significant addition in this phase.
- Real `ConcurrencyScope` support via `AppendOptions.concurrencyScope` and `ConcurrencyScopeBuilder`, and `appendMany` now commits the whole batch through a single atomic RPC instead of one `Append` call per event.
- `getTailSequenceNumber`, `getNextSequenceNumber`, `getTailSequenceNumberForObserver` — the current/next position in the sequence, including relative to the event types a specific reactor/reducer handles.
- `getForEventSourceIdAndEventTypes`, `getFromSequenceNumber` — reading events back for one event source (narrowed by type/stream) or forward from a bookmarked position.
- `completeStream` — closes an event stream type/id pair so it can no longer be appended to.
- `appendOperations` — a hot `Flow` that emits after every completed append made through a specific `IEventSequence` instance.

### `IEventStore` / `IChronicleClient` completeness (this phase)

- `compliance`, `eventTypes`, `namespaces`, `externalServices`, `jobs`, `eventStoreSubscriptions`, `webhooks`, and `identities` are now all on the `IEventStore` interface itself (previously only on the concrete `EventStore` class), plus `getEventSequence(id)` for non-default event sequences.
- `IChronicleClient.getEventStores()` / `evictEventStores()` — list every event store known to the kernel, and clear this client's cached `EventStore` instances without disposing the client.
- `IIdentityManagerService.rename` — renames the human-readable name the kernel has stored for an identity.
- `INamespacesService.getAll()` — lists every namespace in the event store.
- `ChronicleConnectionString.toString()` — renders a parsed connection string back to its textual form; round-trips through `parse()`.

### Transactions, constraints, seeding, read models (this phase)

- Richer `IUnitOfWork`: `isSuccess`, `getConstraintViolations`/`getConcurrencyViolations`/`getAppendErrors`, `onCompleted`, `tryGetLastCommittedEventSequenceNumber`. Richer `IUnitOfWorkManager`: `tryGetFor`, `setCurrent`.
- Constraint scoping — `IConstraintBuilder.perEventSourceType()`/`.perEventStreamType()`/`.perEventStreamId()` narrow a constraint's uniqueness check to a dimension instead of checking globally across the whole event store.
- `IEventSeedingBuilder.forNamespace()` — a scoped builder for seed data targeting a namespace other than the event store's own; typed `forEventType()` for both the top-level and namespace-scoped builders.
- `watch()`/`getSnapshotsById()` now deserialize straight into the caller's read model type instead of raw JSON; `releaseMany` decrypts `@Pii` properties for a batch of instances in one call.

### Samples, docs, and Java interop (both phases)

- Both Kotlin and Java console samples demonstrate every feature above end-to-end, wired into the existing interactive command loop — including, this phase, a single-event redact, a bulk "GDPR erase everything for this customer" redact, constraint scoping, `IdentityManager.rename`, read-model snapshot history, and a live background watcher using typed `watch()`.
- Java bridge parity for all of the above via `io.cratis.chronicle.java.*JavaBridge`, including new bridges for the value-class-typed members Java cannot call directly (`redact`, the event-lookup methods, `completeStream`, `ConcurrencyScopeBuilder.withSequenceNumber`, and a callback-based subscription to `watch`/`appendOperations`).
- New and expanded guide/reference pages (Webhooks, Jobs, Event Type Migrations, Event Store Subscriptions, External Services, EventStore API, Seeding, Configuration, Constraints, Transactions, Read Models, Annotations), with matching validated snippets in both the Kotlin and Java client-snippet trees.

- Fixed a momentary token-endpoint outage failing calls while the cached OAuth token was still valid: the client now falls back to the cached token until it truly expires and throttles failed fetch attempts, so an auth blip no longer drops the session

## Added

- `chronicle://host1:port,host2:port,...` connection strings — the client now connects to any one of several configured hosts instead of only a single server.
- `chronicle+srv://` connection strings, resolving the target host(s) via a DNS SRV lookup, re-resolved on every connect/reconnect so membership changes are picked up automatically. The DNS server to query can be overridden with the `srvNameServer` option.
- A `loadBalancer` connection string option selecting how one address is picked among several candidates: `least-connections` (the default — probes each candidate and picks the one with the fewest active connections), `round-robin`, or `random`.
- A `skipTlsValidation` connection string option to skip TLS certificate validation independently of disabling TLS entirely. Defaults to `true`, matching the client's previous behavior — set `skipTlsValidation=false` to require full certificate chain validation.
- Client connections now report the process id, process path, machine name, and client type to the Chronicle kernel, improving connection diagnostics.

## Changed

- Reconnect backoff is jittered, so a fleet of clients that lost the same kernel does not reconnect in lockstep.
- The client connection ID rotates on every reconnect, so observers re-register under an ID the kernel recognizes.

## Fixed

- The client now reconnects to the kernel instead of staying down. A dropped connection was swallowed by empty catch blocks, so it completed silently with nothing logged and no way to recover short of restarting the application.
- A connection that goes silent without erroring is now detected and reconnected. The kernel does not close the keep-alive stream when it evicts a client, so waiting for an error never fired.
- Reactors and reducers are re-registered on every reconnect. They previously registered once against a connection ID captured at construction, so after any reconnect they observed nothing for the rest of the process lifetime.
- Reactor and reducer observation streams are re-established after they end, instead of that observer stopping permanently. This includes streams the kernel closes deliberately, such as cross-store (inbox) observations.
- Keep-alive and observation failures are now reported instead of being discarded silently.

## Changed

- The client now connects to the Chronicle Kernel over a single port (`35000`) instead of a separate gRPC port plus a management HTTP port (`8080`). The OAuth token endpoint is derived from the connection's own host and port.
- TLS is now enabled by default for local development — the Kernel's consolidated port requires TLS to multiplex gRPC and OAuth/API traffic, so the development connection string and `ChronicleOptions.development()` no longer disable it. The client automatically trusts the Kernel's auto-generated self-signed development certificate.

Any caller that explicitly configured `managementPort` on `ChronicleConnectionString` will need to remove that configuration. Callers connecting to `localhost:35000` for local development no longer need to pass `disableTls=true` — TLS is now on by default and the Kernel's self-signed certificate is trusted automatically.

Projected read models are stored in a collection named after the read model's identifier. Arc's MongoDB integration reads a pluralized collection by default, so a Chronicle projection and an Arc query didn't meet unless the app configured a workaround. .NET avoids this because its client sends `ContainerName` from a naming policy.

**Change (additive, minor)**
- New exported `type ReadModelNamingPolicy = (identifier: string, readModelType?: Constructor) => string`.
- New `ChronicleOptions.readModelNamingPolicy?`, accepted by `fromConnectionString(cs, {...})` and `development({...})`. It flows through `ChronicleClient` → `EventStore` → `Projections` / `Reducers` / `ReadModels`, and each takes it as an optional trailing parameter.
- `buildReadModelDefinition` applies it to `ContainerName` only. `Type.Identifier` and `DisplayName` are unchanged.
  - The read-model class is passed wherever the client knows it: direct and model-bound read models, reducers with a read-model class, and projections whose identifier maps to a known class.
  - The class is `undefined` only where the client has just an identifier, such as a projection with a custom `.containerName('x')`. A policy should fall back to the identifier there.
- **Default:** no policy means `ContainerName` is the identifier, so registration payloads are byte-identical. The registration golden file is untouched.
- `.containerName()` on the projection builder is unchanged. As in .NET, it sets the read model identifier.
- `Documentation/read-models.md` gains a "Container names" section with a snippet.

The Arc.TypeScript Chronicle integration will pass Arc's MongoDB naming policy through this option in a follow-up, so projections land in the collection Arc reads by default.

## Added

## Limitations

- As in the Chronicle kernel, composite values are joined with an unescaped `-`, so values containing `-` can collide across components (for example `['a-b', 'c']` and `['a', 'b-c']`). The scenarios reproduce this behavior (Cratis/Chronicle#4131).
- Nested, indexed or repeated key paths, more than three properties, non-string or missing parts, `ignoreCasing` on booleans, non-ASCII characters under `ignoreCasing` and scoped constraints reject with `UnsupportedEventSequenceOperation`. Use a kernel-backed test for these cases.

## Added

- `EventScenario` and `ReactorScenario` support kernel-verified unique-event-type constraints that span several event types with removal cycles, for unscoped constraints: a source is blocked from a second covered event until one of the constraint's removal events releases the cycle; a removal on another source releases nothing; an event type that is both covered and a removal is checked before it releases, so a blocked one releases nothing. Within a batch, a release recorded by an earlier event lets a later covered event on the same source succeed, and a rejected batch rolls back its releases.
- The supported definitions are one covered type without removal types, two covered types with two separate removal types, and three covered types with three removal types where one type is both. A multi-type definition must be the only constraint definition in the scenario.

## Limitations

- Other combinations of covered and removal types, multi-type definitions alongside other definitions, removal event types without fields, and scoped constraints reject with `UnsupportedEventSequenceOperation`. Use a kernel-backed test for these cases.

## Added

- `EventScenario` and `ReactorScenario` now support kernel-verified unique-property replacement and removal for unscoped constraints. When an event source replaces its claimed value, its old value becomes available to another source. Removal events declared with `@removeConstraint` or fluent `removedWith` release only that source's claim; a wrong-source or repeated removal does not free another owner's value.
- In atomic batches, a release takes effect only after the whole batch succeeds, matching the kernel: a second source cannot reclaim a value released earlier in the same batch, but can reclaim it in a later append.

## Limitations

- Scenarios still reject unresolved removal names, removal event types shared by several definitions, removal of unique-event-type constraints, and scoped, composite, case-insensitive or overlapping definitions with `UnsupportedEventSequenceOperation`. Use a kernel-backed test for these cases.

## Added

- `EventScenario` and `ReactorScenario` now accept a wider, kernel-verified domain for unique-property keys: digits, `.`, `@`, `_`, `-`, `:`, `|`, `{`, `}`, `$`, empty and padded strings, `é`, and schema-backed booleans. Boolean `true` conflicts with the string `"True"` but not `"true"`, as in the kernel. Other values still reject with `UnsupportedEventSequenceOperation`.

## Changed

- A unique-property key must hold a primitive value of its declared type; a `Date` or concept value on a constrained key rejects with `UnsupportedEventSequenceOperation`. Unconstrained properties are unaffected.

## Added

Scenarios reject conflicting appends and preserve atomic batch rollback; committed fixtures verify the supported behavior against the pinned Chronicle kernel.
- The supported subset covers case-sensitive, unscoped unique string properties whose values are nonempty ASCII letters and spaces, and one event type per unique-event constraint. Other key values, such as ones containing digits, `@`, `.` or accented letters, reject with `UnsupportedEventSequenceOperation`. Scoped, case-insensitive, composite or nested, removal, replacement, overlapping, and multi-type unique-event constraints reject with `UnsupportedEventSequenceOperation` instead of being partially simulated. Use a kernel-backed test for those shapes, or set `constraints: 'disabled'` only when the test does not depend on constraints.

When the child's identifier is a discoverable `id`/`Id` or given with `identifiedBy`, and the child key defaults to the event source ID, the identifier comes from the event source ID. ## Added

- `ActivatedArtifact.run(callback, invocation)` now receives an `ArtifactInvocationContext` for every call: the handled event's `EventContext` and handler name, or the replay notification. A host can then run each reactor or reducer invocation in a context that matches that event, for example with its correlation ID.
- `ActivatedArtifact.complete()` is an optional hook called once per activation after its batch has been processed, also when processing failed, and before the delivery is acknowledged. If it rejects, the delivery fails with `ArtifactCompletionFailed`, which keeps a processing error if there was one; `dispose()` still runs afterwards. A host can use it to fail a delivery whose resources could not be released cleanly.

Activators written for the previous release keep working unchanged: the callback passed to `run` still takes no arguments, and both new members are optional.

## Fixed

- Event-context projection mappings and context-derived keys now reach the kernel in the form it resolves, `$eventContext(<Property>)`, as Chronicle for .NET sends them. Previously declarative `toEventContextProperty(...)`, `usingKeyFromContext(...)` and `usingParentKeyFromContext(...)` sent `$context.<name>`, which the kernel doesn't recognize, and model-bound `@setFromContext(...)` sent a bare name that the kernel read as an event content property.
- Invalid event-context paths now fail when the projection is registered, naming the projection, read model and path, instead of failing for every event in the kernel. Registration accepts any `EventContext` property, `causedBy.subject`, `causedBy.name`, `causedBy.userName` and `causedBy.onBehalfOf` as a whole, and `occurred.week()`, the kernel's only derived function. Paths into the `causation` and `tags` collections are rejected. The error's cause, `InvalidEventContextPropertyError`, is exported.

## Added

- Reactor handlers receive a third argument, `services`, with the `eventStore` and `readModels` of the event store and namespace the reactor observes, plus the delivery's abort `signal`. A handler can now append explicitly and check the `AppendResult`, or look up a read model before acting, as reactors in Chronicle for .NET can through injected services.
- `ChronicleOptions.artifactActivator` lets an application or framework construct reactors and reducers, for example from a dependency injection container, like `ClientArtifactsActivator` in .NET. It returns an `ActivatedArtifact` with the instance and optional `run` and `dispose` hooks. With an activator, an artifact is activated once per delivered batch (and separately for replay notifications); `run` wraps each handler call and its returned events, and `dispose` runs when the batch is done. Activation failures fail the partition like handler failures; cleanup failures are logged.

- Without an activator, reactors and reducers are still constructed once per observation with no arguments, exactly as before.
- The reactor documentation covers explicit appends, read-model lookups, activation lifetimes, and replay: `@onceOnly()` keeps a handler out of replay but does not protect against retries or duplicate delivery, so explicit writes should be idempotent. The policy applies to that type's direct child and nested definitions and doesn't cascade further.

The hash used to drop nested keys, so those changes left `LastUpdated` unchanged. The kernel compares definitions by structure, so replays were already triggered correctly; only the `LastUpdated` metadata was wrong.

Brings the read-model and append-wait APIs closer to the Chronicle .NET client, and lets callers cancel a completion wait.

## Added

- `waitForCompletion({ timeoutMs, signal })` accepts an `AbortSignal`. Canceling the signal rejects the wait promptly with the signal's reason and cancels the underlying call, including while the client is still waiting for an access token. Other calls that wait for the same token are not affected. The existing `waitForCompletion(timeoutMs)` form and its five-second default are unchanged.

## Changed

- `getInstanceById` is no longer deprecated. It is the canonical read-by-key API, as `GetInstanceById` is in .NET, and its behavior for a missing instance is documented. `findInstanceById` remains for code that wants `null` when no instance exists.

## Fixed

- A completion wait no longer leaves its timeout timer queued after it finishes or is canceled.
- A stale comment was removed and a sample comment uses American spelling.

## Added

- `RejectedChronicleCredentials`: the client now stops retrying and rejects `getEventStore(...)` and later calls when the credentials are rejected. This applies when the token endpoint answers `invalid_client`, `unauthorized_client`, or `invalid_grant`, or the kernel refuses an API key, on three consecutive attempts. Previously a wrong password made `getEventStore(...)` wait forever.
- `@childrenFrom(Event, ChildType, identifiedBy?, parentKey?)` accepts the child class as its second argument. Use it under runtimes that emit no type metadata, such as `tsx`, so the client knows the element type of a children collection.
- A root `yarn test` script.

## Changed

- Artifact discovery no longer scans `.ts` sources when your program runs as compiled JavaScript. Artifacts register when their modules are imported. When the program runs from TypeScript (a `.ts`, `.tsx`, `.mts`, or `.cts` entry file, Vitest, or a `tsx`, `ts-node`, or type-stripping loader), the default still scans `**/*.ts`, and now also `**/*.tsx`. An explicit `discoveryPatterns` is always used as given.
- `glob` is now a dependency of `@cratis/chronicle`, and `!` patterns in `discoveryPatterns` exclude files as documented. When a discovered file fails to import, the error names the file.
- A failed token request no longer stops the call. The client logs the token endpoint and cause, then sends the call without a token, the same way the .NET client does. A kernel with authentication turned off is therefore reachable, and an unauthenticated rejection reports the token failure. When the kernel rejects a cached token, the client refreshes it and retries the call once.
- With client credentials, tokens are requested from the server the client selected for the connection, not always from the first host in the connection string.
- A declarative join without `.on(...)` now fails when the projection is built, with a clear message. A join inside `.children(...)` uses the children's `identifiedBy` as its default, whatever the call order.
- The keep-alive reports the installed client version instead of `1.0.0`.

## Fixed

- `@setValue(Event, value)`, `.set(...).toValue(value)`, and constant keys now write their value to the read model. They previously sent a form the kernel did not apply, so the property kept its old value.
- Read models with a `@nested` property, or a declarative `.nested(...)`, now register. The kernel previously failed registration with a `NullReferenceException`.
- Read-model queries (`findInstanceById`, `getInstances`, snapshots, watches, and materialized reads) now return every property the model declares. Before, they only returned properties declared with `@field`. Nested plain classes, `ConceptAs` values, dates, and booleans are restored as their declared types.
- With legacy decorators, an event whose properties are constructor parameters without default values, such as `constructor(readonly name: string)`, now registers with its property types. Before, it registered an empty schema, so projections could not map its data.
- A model-bound read model whose mappings are all on properties, such as `@setFrom` without `@fromEvent`, now registers without file discovery. With standard decorators the class registers once an instance exists. Querying it before then fails with a message that says to add a class-level `@fromEvent(...)`.
- Child and nested model types are no longer registered as extra root read models, and two child classes with the same name no longer fail registration.
- A process that registered reactors or reducers now exits after `client.dispose()`.
- `eventStore.externalServices.register(...)` now works against Chronicle 19 kernels, and it rejects when the kernel does not accept the definition. It previously failed with `UNIMPLEMENTED`.
- Token request failures now name the endpoint and the connection error, instead of `No authentication method specified` or an empty message.

They also document the kernel issue where `waitForCompletion()` waits for observers that don't handle the appended event ([Cratis/Chronicle#4132](https://github.com/Cratis/Chronicle/issues/4132)).

Read model watches no longer yield an empty changeset when they start.

## Fixed

- `watch()` skips the kernel's subscription acknowledgment, as the .NET client does. Before, every new watch began with an empty changeset that had no key and no read model. Consumers that built lists from the changesets got an empty entry. Normal changes and removals are unaffected.

Reactors now follow Chronicle for .NET's replay rules. They accept kernel replays by default, and `@onceOnly()` and `@replay()` control what runs during a replay, like the `[OnceOnly]` and `[Replay]` attributes.

## Added

- Class-level `@onceOnly()` registers a reactor as not replayable, so the kernel never replays it. The marker is not inherited, as in .NET.
- Method-level `@onceOnly()` skips that handler when an event is delivered during a replay.
- `@replay()` marks a handler that runs instead of the regular handler for its event type during a replay.
- The shared Chronicle documentation shows TypeScript examples for once-only and replay handlers.

## Changed

- **Reactors are now replayable by default, as in .NET.** Existing reactors accept explicit replays. They also accept kernel-initiated replays, such as rewinds after an event revision or redaction, and replays after a definition change when that option is enabled. Before upgrading, mark reactors that cause side effects with class-level `@onceOnly()`, or mark individual handlers when only those handlers must be skipped.
- Reactor registration fails for a `@replay()` handler that matches no registered event type, and for two replay handlers for the same event type.
- Inherited replay handlers are found, and the most derived method wins.

Adds attribute-style constraint decorators, matching `[Unique]` and `[RemoveConstraint]` in the .NET client. Constraint declarations that share a name are now merged consistently, whichever way they are declared.

- `@unique()` marks an event property or an event class as unique. `@removeConstraint(name)` releases a named constraint, can be repeated, and is inherited like the .NET attribute.
- The shared constraint pages on the Chronicle documentation site now show TypeScript examples for model-bound constraints.

## Changed

- Same-named fluent `uniqueFor` declarations across classes, together with decorated event types of the same name, are merged into one definition. Before, each registered its own definition with the same name.
- `hasFor` looks constraints up by their registered name, as `HasFor` does in .NET.
- A message configured with `withMessage` now replaces the kernel's message in append results.

## Fixed

- Two `@constraint` classes with the same id now fail at registration. Before, the last one silently replaced the first.
- Merging same-named constraints with conflicting scopes or ignore-casing settings now fails with a clear error.
- The first message supplied among same-named unique event type declarations is kept.
- A `$` in a violation value is inserted literally into the message.

Known limitation: fluent `withName()` is not sent to the kernel (#91). The documentation says so.

Read models are discovered from `@projection`, `@reducer` and model-bound property mappings, as in Chronicle for .NET, which has no read-model attribute. This PR removes the last guidance that still pointed to the deprecated `@readModel` decorator.

## Changed

- The README, documentation, JSDoc and console samples now use inferred read models instead of the deprecated `@readModel` decorator. Existing applications need no changes, and `@readModel` is still supported.

## Fixed

- An inferred variant read model now uses the model's own members when its shared-handler mappings are validated.

- Read models are recognized from the projections, reducers and model-bound projection decorators that build them, the way the .NET client discovers them, so a read-model class needs no extra decorator. Use `static readModelId` on the class to choose a custom identifier.

- Registering two read models with the same identifier fails with an error instead of letting one silently replace the other.

- `reactorResultHandler` in `ChronicleOptions` lets an application handle values a reactor returns that are not events, for example commands for a CQRS framework to execute. The handler receives the returned value, the triggering `EventContext`, the reactor type, the event store name and the namespace, and returns `true` when it handled the whole result or `false` to let Chronicle append the events it recognizes. A handler that throws fails the partition, so a side effect is never acknowledged without having run.

- `readModels.getInstanceById` is deprecated in favor of `findInstanceById`; its behavior is unchanged.

## Fixed

- `appendMany` sends every supplied concurrency scope label, not only the scopes derived from the events' event source ids.
- An event store now uses the `clientArtifactsProvider` configured in `ChronicleOptions` instead of always using the default artifact discovery.
- Causation links added while appending no longer leak into sibling operations.

## Security

- Reading a read model that holds personal data now fails when the data cannot be released, instead of returning the unreleased values.

## Added

- Declare event types, read models, projections, reducers, reactors and the other SDK artifacts with TC39 standard decorators, without enabling `experimentalDecorators`. Legacy decorators keep working.
- Schema support for explicitly typed arrays and for Guid-, Date-, and primitive-backed concepts, with a `static readonly valueType` hint for concepts when no decorator type metadata is emitted.

## Changed

- Standard-mode schema errors are collected and reported together before the client registers any artifact with the Kernel.
- Documentation shows standard-mode `@field` declarations and labels constructor-property examples as legacy-mode.

## Fixed

- Member-less events and read models work in standard mode.
- An explicit `@field(Object)` keeps its object schema, and concepts and Guids are recognized across duplicate `@cratis/fundamentals` copies.

## Fixed

- Load `@cratis/chronicle` and every exported subpath directly in Node.js ESM without a bundler. Published JavaScript and declaration files now use explicit `.js` file specifiers, and each build verifies the packed package imports natively.
- Preserve constraint violations and errors when a batch append is rejected before sequence numbers are assigned, so a rejected batch no longer reports an empty result set.

## Fixed

- Repeated `removedWith()` calls on a unique property constraint now retain every distinct release event, so any declared event can free the value instead of only the last one (#77).
- Unique event-type release examples now explicitly state that the TypeScript client does not support that workflow, rather than demonstrating a constraint that enforced nothing.

## Added

- `@encrypted()` decorator (`@cratis/chronicle/confidentiality`) for values that need encryption at rest without being personal data subject to GDPR right-to-erasure — an API key, a webhook signing secret, a partner credential (Cratis/Chronicle#4095)
- `EncryptionScope.Subject` (default), `.Namespace`, and `.Global` — the identity an `@encrypted()` value's key is provisioned under. A subject-scoped key is always disjoint from any `@pii()` key for the same subject; a namespace-scoped key is shared by every value marked that way in one event store namespace; a global-scoped key is shared across the whole installation

Ports Chronicle's read model variations feature (Cratis/Chronicle#3956, shipped for the .NET
client in Cratis/Chronicle#4062, and for Kotlin/Java in Cratis/Chronicle.Kotlin#85) to the
TypeScript client, with documentation snippets for both authoring styles.

## Added (model-bound)

- `@variantOf(identity, key)` declares a read model to be one of several mutually exclusive
  representations of the same logical entity. Entering one variant removes the entity from every
  sibling variant.
- `@entersOn(eventType, key?)` names the event(s) that may create/resurrect a variant. Every other
  event a variant projects from — whether via `@fromEvent`/`@setFrom` directly or through
  `@globalFor` — is automatically reclassified into an update-only join, so it can update an
  already-active instance but can never create or resurrect one.
- `@globalFor(identity)` shares a mapping across every variant of a group without repeating it on
  each variant class. A shared mapping that targets a member some variant lacks is a declaration
  error (`GlobalHandlerPropertyNotOnVariant`), not a silently skipped mapping. A class decorated
  only with `globalFor` is discovered through a new `IClientArtifactsProvider.globalForHandlers`
  member and is never registered as its own projection.

## Added (declarative)

- The fluent builder gets the equivalent shape: `builder.variantOf(identity, m => m.key).entersOn(EventType)`,
  with `.from(...)` for any other event reclassified the same way.
- There is no declarative equivalent of `@globalFor`, matching the .NET and Kotlin clients — a
  shared mapping is repeated per variant builder.

Cross-wiring (which sibling's entering events remove this variant) runs once per `register()`
call, over every variant discovered in that call, mirroring the other clients' reclassifier.

## Note on current kernel support

A variant's own key property is what the reclassified self-join correlates on. The kernel does not
honor `$eventSourceId` in a property mapping yet (Cratis/Chronicle#3924 — a pre-existing gap that
already affects `fromEvent`'s `key`/`toEventSourceId` generally, not something introduced here).
The definition shape this ships is otherwise complete and verified; it starts working end-to-end
the day that is fixed, with no changes needed on this side.

## Changed

- **Breaking:** an append no longer sends client-chosen route defaults. An unspecified source type, stream type, or stream identifier is omitted, and the kernel resolves it to source type `Default`, stream type `All`, and stream identifier `Default`. Previously the client wrote source type `Default`, stream type `Default`, and the event source identifier as the stream identifier, so existing streams are no longer continued by default.
- **Breaking:** route-scoped reads no longer narrow to that legacy route either. `getTailSequenceNumber()`, `getNextSequenceNumber()`, `getTailSequenceNumberForObserver()`, and `getForEventSourceIdAndEventTypes()` leave an unsupplied dimension unnarrowed. Without this, every event written by the new append path was invisible to those reads — a narrowed read returned an empty collection and a narrowed tail returned the unset sentinel, with no error. Supplied dimensions are still sent unchanged, and `getFromSequenceNumber()`/`hasEventsFor()` carry no route dimensions at all.
- To keep writing to and reading from an existing stream, pass all three dimensions explicitly — `append(id, event, { sourceType: 'Default', streamType: 'Default', streamId: id })` and `getForEventSourceIdAndEventTypes(id, types, 'Default', id)`. [Preserve existing append routes](Documentation/migrate-append-routing.md) covers both halves.
- Event contexts now preserve the kernel's routing metadata (`eventSourceType`, `eventStreamType`, `eventStreamId`, `subject`, occurrence time, correlation, causation, tags, identity, hash, observation state) across reads, reactors, and reducers.
- The client refuses to write to a server whose contract is incompatible, or that has no compatibility check at all. The verdict is permanent rather than retried, including for a server reached during a background reconnect, and authorization verdicts are read as the kernel sends them.
- Contracts pinned to the released `@cratis/chronicle.contracts` 18.4.1.

Upgrade every kernel node to 18.4.1 (or later) **before** upgrading this client. The client checks its installed contract descriptor against the server before a connection is considered usable and before event-sequence operations, so an older kernel is rejected rather than written to.

## `EventSequence` wiring

`append` and `appendMany` now pull identity, causation chain, and correlation ID from the singletons instead of hard-coded `[System]` / empty values:

```ts
// Before (all hard-coded)
CausedBy: { Subject: '5d032c92-...', Name: '[System]', ... }
Causation: [{ Type: 'TypeScriptClient.Append', ... }]

// After (context-aware)
identityProvider.setCurrentIdentity(new Identity(sub, name, userName));
causationManager.add(CausationType.appendEvent, { eventType: id });

// EventSequence picks up whatever is in the current async context
const identity = identityProvider.getCurrent();
const causationChain = causationManager.getCurrentChain();
const correlationId = correlationIdManager.current;
```

## Added

- `then no readmodel <ReadModel> for <key>` asserts that the instance with that key does not exist. The key is required and must match the read model's identifier type, and a present and an absent assertion for the same instance are reported as a contradiction. See [Specifications](https://github.com/Cratis/Screenplay/blob/main/Documentation/screenplay/specifications.md). (#284)
- Models that use the assertion compile to ESM v5 (language and semantics `5.0`, `schemaVersion` 5). Models without it keep their v1–v4 canonical bytes and revisions. ESM consumers must admit v5 explicitly before they read such a model.
- The reference runner checks absence for projection-backed read models. For read models built by a reducer it returns `SemanticUnsupported`, so a target provider must check the deletion instead of reporting a pass.
- The editor grammar, completion and keyword help, and the MCP inspection tools recognise absence assertions.
- Typed workspace authoring binds each member of a composite absence key to the read model's identifier type. Safe authoring rejects new key members that don't resolve, keeps unchanged existing ones, and accepts explicit repairs of a key member, an enclosing member or the keyed query's `by` identifier. A declaration edit, such as changing a property's type, can repair an unresolved key member but is refused in both modes if it would retarget or unbind a resolved one. Draft authoring accepts new unresolved key members and reports them as reference debt.
- Renaming a composite-type property also renames the absence-key members bound to it. A rename is refused while an absence key in the workspace is unresolved.
