- Document that C# code bodies use provider-generated PascalCase member names, while authored Screenplay identifiers remain unchanged. The portable default tenant remains the zero GUID; provider-side tenant translation is still pending. Refs #282.
- Decision records 0012 and 0018 now use the supported `implemented` stage and retain their outstanding provider-verification notes.

## Fixed

- Comments before or on a template's `fits slot` line stay with that directive when printed canonically or moved with `expand-layout`. The typed JSON syntax is unchanged. (#276)
- Comments on contribution navigation lines and on declaration and screen file references also stay with their lines.

## Added

- Screenplay publishes typed-context descriptors: language-neutral data describing exactly what each code body can see, so providers such as Stage can generate typed wrappers instead of `dynamic` contexts. They cover reducer transitions (a typed `Event` per `on` event using its current generation, and a nullable `State` shaped like the read model), validation and rule code, code policies at each place they are used, and the context of command handlers, which are still not bound. This is the descriptor part of decision 0012 and advances #139.
- `CompilationResult` exposes the descriptors through `TypedContextDescriptors` and `ContextsFor(requirementId)`. `IsWrapperReady` is true only for descriptors from a successful compilation whose types all resolve; a failed compilation publishes only command-handler descriptors, marked not ready. Every descriptor carries the definitions of the concept and composite types it refers to.
- MCP has a paged `typed-contexts` view; `implementation-requirements` items gain a small `typedContext` reference (count and operation ids).
- The descriptor contract has its own revision (1), a published vocabulary of portable type tokens and source kinds, and two readable vectors (`typed-contexts-v1.json`, `unbound-handler-context-v1.json`) packaged with the canonical vectors. Canonical executable-model bytes and revisions are unchanged.

Six shape choices were decided under the maintainer's delegation: descriptors are a sidecar, never part of canonical executable-model bytes; types use portable tokens; policy descriptors are per use site; derived values such as `IsFirst` are included and marked as derived; command-handler descriptors describe only the context and appear only when the command's shape resolves; and descriptors have their own versioned contract.

## Added

- `SemanticEvaluator.EstablishWorld(plan, facts)` establishes a deterministic reference world from ordered existing facts, with no read-model snapshots required. It checks every fact first: a default or null fact array, an unknown event, a payload that doesn't match the event, a missing or blank event-source identity, a source type other than the event's declared producer destination type, or a blank tag returns `SemanticRejected` with category `Contract`. A fact that affects a reducer-backed read model returns `SemanticUnsupported` with capability `Projection`, because reducer transitions are opaque. This is reference semantics and does not replace Chronicle replay. (#253)

## Changed

- Specification `given` events now go through the same establishment path. Existing specification outcomes are unchanged.

## Changed

- A valid `persona` no longer stops a model from binding to the executable model. It is reported as information only, and models that already bound produce the same bytes. Personas and providers are still not part of the executable model; the authentication documentation describes where a renderer reads provider identities from the compilation result. This is part of #254.
- A persona whose policy cannot be resolved is now an error in compilation, Safe authoring and executable binding, so it never falls back to anonymous access. Draft authoring still accepts it and reports the unresolved reference.

## Fixed

- A value indented under a clock trigger (`every …`, `at …`) reports `PLAY0450`, because clock triggers take no values. (#258)
- A line indented under a `reads` line reports `PLAY0451`. It no longer becomes a property of the command or a value of the reaction trigger. (#259)

## Added

- A `StateView` slice's specification can use `when append … for`, as long as exactly one command produces the event and so determines the source type. (#262)

## Changed

- PLAY0284 follows what Chronicle fills in a join. It counts a join's mapped fields and compatible AutoMap fields instead of the join's label, which Chronicle discards. It no longer counts a field that AutoMap cannot fill because an explicit mapping already uses the same event field. It also no longer counts fields that only a join inside a `nested` block would fill, because Chronicle does not currently apply joins there. Models that relied on those cases now get PLAY0284 for fields that stay empty at runtime. (#262)

## Fixed

- The documentation now describes what the executable model binds: one `then error` per specification, `produces … for` only on the command's identifier, and `all` projections keyed per event source instead of global counters. The shapes it rejects now get clearer diagnostics. (#261)

## Fixed

- Canonical printing and `expand-layout` keep comments inside `form` blocks, including `@input` notes and comments on `populate`, fields, `on submit` and inline `on` behaviors, in order and without duplicates. (#267)
- Comments on navigation lines inside screen actions and tables stay with their lines when printed canonically.

## Added

- Event generations now bind to the executable model. Events with several generations share one contract identity and carry their complete prior revisions, predecessor links and revision-specific property identities. Ordinary references use the current generation. This implements decisions 0011 and 0015 and advances #71.
- Persisted event contracts can advance through an explicit, catalog-revision-checked workspace transaction. Renaming or moving an event preserves its identities across generations; combining a rename with evolution still requires explicit advancement.
- The RegisterProject v2 canonical corpus declares two event generations, removes the duplicated `projectId` from the current event payload and uses the event source as its identity. Single-file, folder, reordered and relocated forms produce the same model. This advances #168.

## Changed

- Models with multiple event generations select ESM v4. A lone `generation 1` keeps its previous ESM version, and v1–v3 canonical bytes are unchanged. Consumers must explicitly admit v4 before accepting these models; generation transformations, historical replay and Chronicle deployment support remain separate work under #71.
- ESM v4 no longer serializes projection-transition cardinality and rejects the legacy `ZeroOrOne` and `Many` values. Query cardinality is unchanged (decision 0007; part of #132).
- References to removed current-generation properties fail binding instead of falling back to historical shapes. MCP understands generation-qualified addresses and exports canonical v4 models.

## Added

- MCP can export the compiled executable model: `read-workspace` view `executable-model` returns its schema, language and semantic versions, model revision and size, plus bounded base64 pages of the exact canonical bytes. It is available only when compilation succeeded; otherwise it reports `available: false` and points to the `executable-diagnostics` view. Continuation pages must pass `expectedModelRevision` and `expectedAttachmentManifestRevision`, and are refused if the model or any attached code changed, including a code edit that changes neither the workspace nor the model revision. The exported model alone is not a proof of equivalence or a runnable attachment bundle (decision 0016).
- `implementation-requirements` responses include the attachment-manifest revision. Passing it back pins a continuation and refuses it if attached code changed; continuations without it work as before.

## Added

- MCP can propose a fix for a diagnostic: `read-workspace` has a `repairs` view listing the compiler-authored repairs for the workspace's diagnostics (code, subject and typed operations), and `propose-repair` turns one into a retained proposal. Review it with `read-proposal` and write it with `apply`; nothing is written before that, and a stale workspace revision is refused with a typed conflict.
- The first repair migrates a deprecated `validate csharp` block (`PLAY0397`) to a tagged ```` ```csharp ```` fence. The code body, its requirement identity and content hash, and the executable model are unchanged. The repair reprints the whole file canonically, so it is refused if that would drop a comment. Other `PLAY0397` forms are not offered a repair.
- Library hosts can find and propose repairs through `WorkspaceDiagnosticRepairs.Find` and `ProposeRepair`, which require canonical formatting (`RequiredFormatting`).
- Adding a node whose references don't resolve is refused under the safe reference policy, which is how decision 0014 covers "link" in #138.

## Added

- Events can declare their generations: `event ProjectRegistered generation 2`. An event without the marker is generation 1 and prints as before. Each earlier generation is a complete declaration in the same slice, numbered consecutively from 1; an invalid, duplicate or missing generation is a compile error (`PLAY0446`, `PLAY0447`, `PLAY0448`). Printing, workspace and MCP authoring, and editor highlighting, completion and hover support the marker. This is the grammar part of decision 0011 for #71.
- A model that uses the marker does not compile to the executable model yet: binding fails with `PLAY0449` until generation lineage ships (decision 0015). Models without the marker are unchanged.

## Changed

- Two unmarked declarations of the same event in one slice are now a syntax error (`PLAY0447`, a duplicate generation 1); before, only binding rejected them.
- References to an event and the checks on its shape (produced mappings, specifications, projections, reaction trigger values) use the current, highest generation.
- Tools that read `EventSyntax` directly will now see one declaration per generation. Until the executable model carries lineage, they should reject or skip events that carry a generation marker (`HasGenerationMarker`).

## Added

- Screenplay can show which read-model instances each projection event affects, derived from the executable model with no new syntax: one instance by key (`from`, removal), one per event source (`all`), or many through a root join (instances whose join property equals the event source id, never creating one) or a child join and `remove via join` (children whose identity equals the key, across every parent). `SemanticAffectedProjectionInstances.GetAffectedInstances` returns the relationships per event and block, with an overload that uses the application's types to resolve a child identity. This is the first part of decision 0007 for #132.

## Changed

- A join inside `children` now matches children by their identity, as Chronicle does, instead of by the join's `on` property. Specifications where they differ may produce different results.

## Deprecated

- `ZeroOrOne` and `Many` on a projection transition have no Chronicle meaning. An executable model that carries them, built in code or read from canonical bytes, reports warning `PLAY0445`; they will be removed in the next model version. Models compiled from `.play` sources never carry them.

## Added

- `read-workspace` has a paged `source-map` view: the compiler's map from each semantic id to its role, identity origin, document and exact source span. When compilation did not succeed it reports `available: false` and points to the `executable-diagnostics` view instead of returning an empty map.
- `find-fixtures` finds the payload values and `for` destinations of `when append` events, with the role `whenAppendedEvent`.
- Compact specification summaries show a `then denied` assertion and the appended event of a `when append` specification.

## Fixed

- `find-assertion-gaps` no longer reports a slice whose only assertion is `then denied` as unasserted.
- References and dependencies to an appended event are labelled `whenAppendedEvent` instead of `thenEvent`.
- The server's initialize instructions say identities persist when a proposal is applied; `export-workspace` is optional, for transfer or backup.

## Added

- Reaction triggers can declare the views they decide from: `reads <View> [as <alias>] [by <trigger value>]`, with the same alias rules as command reads. Parsing, validation, printing, the syntax walker, MCP references, and editor highlighting, completion and hover all support it.
- Diagnostics for trigger reads: an unknown view, a repeated view without an alias, a duplicate alias, an alias that collides with a trigger value, a `by` that names no trigger value (`PLAY0442`, warning), a `by` under a clock trigger (`PLAY0443`, error), and a primitive type read as a view (`PLAY0444`, warning, pointing to `@reads`).

## Changed

- A trigger value named `reads` must now be written `@reads`. A bare `reads` line or `reads <PrimitiveType>` under a trigger reports a diagnostic that names the escape instead of being misread.
- Clock triggers (`every`, `at`) can read whole views but cannot use `by`, since they take no values.
- Neither command nor reaction reads bind at runtime yet; editor guidance says so. `for each <View>` stays reserved.

This is the grammar part of #69 (decision 0006).

Code written inside a Screenplay document can now be mapped back to the exact characters it came from, so a host editor that hands a body to a language service (C#, TypeScript, SQL) can put completions, hovers and diagnostics on the right place in the `.play` file. Screenplay supplies the mapping data; the language service stays in the host editor, as decision 0002 says.

## Added

- `CodeBlockSyntax.BodyStartOffset`, `BodyEndOffset`, `BodyStart`, `BodyEnd` and `BodyLines`: the body's span in the document (UTF-16 offsets, BOM-less, as editors address text) and, for each body line, the original line and the column where its content starts after the common indentation is removed. This covers fenced bodies with a language info string and the legacy tag-line form, CRLF documents, tabs, blank and under-indented lines, and bodies at the end of a file.
- `SemanticImplementationRequirement.BodySpan` and `BodyLines` (`SemanticImplementationBodySpan`, `CodeBlockSourceLine`): the same map for each implementation attachment. A file attachment whose contents were supplied spans the whole file; an unresolved file attachment and an inline body without parser positions have no span.
- The MCP `implementation-requirements` views (workspace and proposal) return `bodySpan` and `bodyLines`, run-length encoded where consecutive lines share a column, so a long body stays within a page.

## Changed

- `CodeBlockSyntax` and `SemanticImplementationRequirement` compare body line maps by value, so two parses of the same text are equal. Positions do not take part in syntax structural equality, so moving a body inside a document never produces a workspace change on its own.

Canonical ESM bytes are unchanged; the map is tooling data, not model meaning.

Policies written as code now bind to the executable semantic model instead of being rejected. This is the third implementation-attachment role from decision 0002, after reducer transitions and rule predicates; proposed decision record 0005 records the role and its composition rule. It also fixes two places where the language silently dropped an authorization condition.

## Added

- A `policy` with a `csharp` body or a `file` binds as an opaque policy-predicate attachment with a stable requirement id and the capability `pure` (`SemanticOpaquePolicyCondition`). A model that has one is ESM v3, like models with reducer bodies or code validation; other models keep their bytes.
- `SemanticExecutionCapability.Authorization`, reported when authorization cannot be decided without running policy code.
- PLAY0440: a policy combines `require` with an inline code block or a file. A policy has one form or the other.
- PLAY0441: a policy has more than one `require` line. Combine the conditions with `and`/`or` in one `require`.
- Proposed decision record 0005: policy predicates as an implementation-attachment role, and authored-order composition.

## Changed

- The reference evaluator does not run policy code. Authorization is evaluated left to right in authored order, as Stage renders it (`&&`/`||`) and Arc evaluates it (in declaration order, stopping at the first false): a portable operand that decides first still decides (`Portable and Custom` denies when `Portable` denies), but once policy code would run, the outcome is unsupported, never allowed or denied. The same order applies across module, feature and construct gates. A specification whose outcome depends on policy code never passes.
- The documented `IsAdultCustomer` example no longer reads the clock or throws on a malformed claim: it uses `context.Occurred` and `DateTime.TryParse`.

## Fixed

- A command or query with two or more `authorize` lines kept only the last one, so every earlier gate was silently dropped. The lines now combine with AND in authored order, as module and feature gates already did and as the documentation states. Printing writes them as one `authorize A and B` line. This makes such commands and queries stricter.
- A policy with two `require` lines silently kept only the last condition. This is now PLAY0441.
- A policy combining `require` with code bound only the code and dropped the condition once policies with code were admitted; this is now PLAY0440 at parse time.

Code kept in files (`file Reducers/Balance.cs`, `file Validations/...`) is now identified by its content when a host reads it from disk, as decision 0002 requires, instead of being reported unresolved. The MCP server does this for every model it opens; `cratis render` can do the same with one call.

## Added

- `AttachmentFiles.Load(root, documents)` reads the files named by a model's implementation attachments (reducer rules, validation rules and code validation, command handlers, policies, reactions, query performers, file constraints) from a model root and returns their contents with warning diagnostics for anything it refuses. Pass `Contents` to `SemanticDocumentSet.Create(documents, catalog, contents)`.
- `ScreenplayWorkspace.WithAttachmentContents(contents, diagnostics)` and a matching `ScreenplayWorkspace.Create` overload carry host-supplied contents through every workspace compilation, proposal and transaction. The workspace itself never reads files, and its revision and serialized bytes do not depend on attachment contents.
- PLAY0430–PLAY0434 warnings for an attachment that is refused or missing: a path that is absolute or leaves the model root, a link, a missing file, a file over 2 MiB (or a set over 8 MiB), and content that is not UTF-8 text. A refused attachment stays unresolved; it never fails a model that compiled before.

## Changed

- The MCP server loads attachment contents from its trusted root, so `implementation-requirements` shows a content hash for each file attachment, and a changed attachment changes its hash. Unchanged attachments reuse the analyzed workspace, and proposals survive an attachment edit.
- `SemanticDocumentSet.Create` normalizes attachment keys, so `./X.cs`, `.\X.cs` and `X.cs` name the same attachment and hash. Two supplied keys that normalize to the same path with different contents are treated as a conflict, not resolved by picking one.
- `PlayFileCompiler` and the standalone Tool compile syntax only and do not read attachments; the documentation now says so (#244).

## Security

- Attachment reads are confined to the model root. Paths are normalized and rejected if absolute, drive- or UNC-qualified, escaping the root with `..`, containing control characters, or naming a Windows device (`CON`, `NUL`, `COM1`, ...). Links and reparse points on the file or any directory of its path are refused, and the resolved path is checked against the root again before reading.
- Only regular files are read. On Linux and macOS the file type is checked with `lstat` before opening, so a FIFO or device cannot block the MCP server or CLI; where the type cannot be verified, the attachment is refused with a warning. Sizes are checked before reading.
- Only a SHA-256 of an attachment's content leaves the loader; contents are never shown, logged or persisted, and diagnostics name only the authored path. Link checks run before opening and after reading, but not as one atomic no-follow open, so a concurrent local writer could swap a link during the read; `file-references.md` documents this.

Validation written as code now binds to the executable semantic model instead of being rejected. This is the second implementation-attachment role from decision 0002, after reducer transitions; it removes the code-validation blocker tracked in #209.

## Added

- A named rule with a `csharp` body or a `file` on a command property or a concept (`invoiceNumber rule BeUnusedInvoiceNumber file Validations/BeUnusedInvoiceNumber.cs`), and a command's `validate csharp` block, bind as opaque rule-predicate and code-validation attachments. Each carries what it guards, its message (including `$strings` keys) and severity, a stable requirement id and the capability `pure`. A bare named rule with neither body nor file is still rejected.
- `SemanticCodeValidation`, `SemanticCommand.CodeValidations`, `SemanticValidationRule.Name` and `SemanticValidationRule.RequirementId`, and the `SemanticValidationRuleKind` members `RulePredicate` and `CodeValidation`.

## Changed

- ESM v3 now means "ESM with implementation attachments": a model is v3 when it has a reducer with a body or code validation. Models with neither keep their v1 or v2 bytes exactly.
- The reference evaluator cannot run code validation. Executing a command guarded by it, directly or through a concept on one of its properties (including inside composite types and collections), reports an unsupported outcome naming the command or concept and the rule, and a specification that runs it never passes. Authorization is still evaluated first, so a `then denied` specification on such a command keeps working. Specifications that do not run the command are unaffected.
- A model with two validation attachments sharing a requirement id is rejected, as duplicate reducer transitions already were.

## Fixed

- An ESM v3 model (released in v4.26.0 for reducers with a body) lost v2 execution semantics: produced facts carried no event-source context, so `then <Event> for …` assertions failed, and a mismatched typed `when … for` was not rejected. v3 models now execute with all v2 semantics, as documented.

Reducers whose transitions are written in the model now bind to the executable semantic model, and every piece of code the model hands off to gets a stable identity. This implements decision 0002 for reducers; the rule-predicate role (code validation) follows.

## Added

- A reducer whose every `on <Event>` rule has a body, inline or in a `file`, binds to a reducer contract in the executable semantic model: the read model it builds, the events it consumes, a key fixed to the event source id, no initial state, and a result that is the new state or a delete, as Chronicle runs reducers. Inline and file bodies bind to the same contract. The body stays opaque code, not portable meaning.
- ESM v3. A model is serialized as v3 only when it contains a bodied reducer; every other model keeps its v1 or v2 bytes exactly. v3 includes all of v2. `LanguageVersion.V3`, `SemanticVersion.V3` and `EsmSchemaV3Support` describe it, and a full v3 golden vector pins its canonical form. Reducer transitions are canonicalized by event, so reordering `on` rules does not change a model's revision.
- Implementation requirements carry `RequirementId` (derived from the owning construct, role and member, never from a path), `ContextVersion` and `ResultVersion`, `RequiredCapability` (`pure` for reducer transitions) and `AttachmentResolution`.
- `SemanticDocumentSet.Create(documents, catalog, attachmentContents)` lets a host supply the contents of `file` attachments, which are then identified by a hash of their content. Without supplied contents a file attachment is reported as `UnresolvedFile` with no hash; the file compiler, MCP server and Tool supplying contents is tracked in #244.
- PLAY0398: a reducer mixes rules with and without a body.
- PLAY0399: a reducer has more than one rule for the same event.

## Changed

- The reference runner does not compute reducer state. A specification that reads a reducer-built read model, through `given readmodel`, `then readmodel` or `then query`, reports an unsupported outcome naming the reducer and never passes; other specifications in the model run as before. Calling the evaluator directly reports the same for a query over, or returned state of, a reducer-built read model.
- A file-backed implementation attachment is no longer hashed from its path, so moving a file no longer changes its hash and editing it is no longer invisible.
- A consumer that accepts only ESM v1 or v2 now receives a v3 model for documents with bodied reducers, where binding used to fail with "requires a portable reducer contract". Reducers without bodies are still rejected with the same message.

A command can read the same view more than once by naming each read. This is the first increment of decision 0003; the executable semantic model still does not bind `reads` (the runtime mapping waits on Cratis/Chronicle#4138).

## Added

- `reads <View> as <alias> [by <property>]` names a read, so a command can read the same view twice, for example `reads Account as source by fromId` and `reads Account as destination by toId`. A `require` path can use the alias as its qualifier: `require source.balance >= amount`.
- PLAY0410: a command reads the same view more than once and not every read has an alias.
- PLAY0411: two reads of one command use the same alias.
- PLAY0412: a reads alias has the same name as one of the command's properties.
- `ReadsSyntax.Alias`, an init-only property, carries the alias in the syntax tree, syntax JSON, the printer, the TextMate grammar and the Monaco language package (completion, keyword docs, symbols).

## Changed

- A `require` path qualified with a view the command reads more than once now says to use one of that view's aliases and lists them, instead of claiming the command does not read the view.
- PLAY0175 also reports `as`, `by` or `reads` used as an alias. Aliases, like `by` properties, are lower-case identifiers.
- Decision 0003 notes that its runtime precondition is only partly met (tracked in Cratis/Chronicle#4138).

## Deprecated

- PLAY0176 is retired and no longer reported. Two identical `reads` lines used to give one PLAY0176 with the second line dropped; now both lines are kept and reported as PLAY0410. The `DiagnosticCodes.DuplicateReads` constant remains for compatibility.

## Changed

- The invoicing sample, the language's largest example, now declares every read model, type and event it uses and gives its authorized specifications an explicit caller. It binds to the executable semantic model with only the unsupported constructs it shows on purpose left, and a specification pins that list so the sample cannot drift from the language again (#240)

## Fixed

- A specification that uses a read model with no keyed query in `given readmodel` or `then readmodel` no longer reports a second error, "must state its identifier property ''", at every block. The one error where the read model is declared, which says why it cannot be identified, remains.

On a case-insensitive filesystem (the macOS default, Windows), moving `app.play` to `App.play` through MCP was refused as `DestinationOccupied`, because the new name already "exists": it is the same file. The refusal lost no data, but it blocked a legitimate rename.

## Fixed

- An MCP apply that renames a document only by case now succeeds and leaves the file with the new casing on disk. A destination is allowed only when it is the same on-disk entry as the document being moved away. A different file whose name differs only by case is still refused, and a failed case-only rename rolls back to the original name.

Folder workspaces now report conflicting owners precisely, and folder conversion is proven to preserve complete semantics and comments.

## Added

- A workspace transaction that finds two files declaring the same thing returns a typed `ConflictingOwner` conflict naming both paths, instead of a generic compilation failure. Ownership belongs to the file that declares a member, never to a module or feature header restated to place a child (#137)
- Specs pin the round trip of a commented model between a single document and a folder: same semantic revision, same identities, same canonical print, and every comment kept. A folder write is rejected before touching disk when the source changed since the proposal (#137)

## Changed

- `PlayFileWriter.Expand` uses the same folder-layout projection as workspace layout changes. `folders.md` explains which parts of `PlayFileCompiler.CompileFolder` and `WriteTo` stay independent of the workspace and why (#137)

Specifications can now start from an event instead of a command, and state how strictly their outcomes are compared. The executable model also reports exactly which inline code and code files a document depends on, and policies can name a code file.

## Added

- `when append <Event>` specifications: the event goes through append-time constraints and projections, then the stated read models and query results are compared. If the specification asserts events, they must equal the complete set of new facts. Reactions do not run.
- Explicit comparison qualifiers on specification outcomes. Event order defaults to authored order and can be relaxed; read-model and query properties default to subset matching and can be made exact. Conflicting actions and malformed qualifiers are reported (`PLAY0358`, `PLAY0359`).
- An inventory of the code attachments the executable model cannot run yet: command handlers and validation, concept validation, rule and policy predicates, reducer transitions, query performers and reactions. Each is listed with its role, owning declaration, language or file, content hash and source location. It sits on the compilation result, and MCP pages it by workspace revision. Binding still fails closed with `PLAY0268`.
- A `policy` may name its implementation with `file <Path>`, as an alternative to inline code. The executable model treats it like a code policy.

Policies become executable. A declarative policy (authenticated, role, claim matches) now binds into the semantic model, and the reference executor evaluates it before validation. A specification can state who the caller is and assert that a caller is denied.

## Added

- Declarative policies bind into the executable semantic model and are evaluated for commands and queries. A command's or query's effective authorization is its own policies, every enclosing feature's and its module's, combined by AND (#142)
- Specifications accept a `given caller` block (`authenticated`, `role "<role>"`, `claim "<type>" = "<value>"`; a claim may repeat) and a `then denied` outcome, distinct from `then error`. A denied command or query is rejected as `Unauthorized` before validation runs (#142)

## Changed

- Claim types compare case-insensitively; role names and claim values compare exactly; a claim carried more than once matches when any of its values matches. A missing claim, a null target or an unresolvable subject denies. This matches how Arc evaluates authorization through .NET's `ClaimsPrincipal`, and `Identity.ClaimValue`/`ClaimValues` now look claim types up case-insensitively too (#142)
- A specification that exercises an authorized command without a `given caller` is reported when binding. Caller identity is never inferred (#142)

`csharp` policies remain a blocking disposition until constrained implementation bodies are defined.

This release tightens how the language is documented and checked. Modules and features can declare authorization, inline code blocks name their language on the fence, and inline code can read its context through typed accessors. The canonical corpus gains vectors for reordered and relocated sources, ESM v2 and fail-closed rejection. Documentation is now checked against the parsers, links and navigation.

## Added

- Modules and features accept `authorize`. It combines by AND with the policies of every command and query beneath them, and folder files merge it like behaviors; a repeated identical clause warns with `PLAY0394` (#75)
- Inline code blocks carry their language as a fence info string (` ```csharp `). The previous forms — a language line above a bare fence, and `validate csharp` — still parse with a `PLAY0397` warning, and printing writes the new form (#184)
- Typed accessors beside every `dynamic` context member (`CommandAs<T>()`, `ArgumentsAs<T>()`, `ArtifactAs<T>()`, …), so LINQ in inline code binds at compile time. A payload of another type throws `ContextPayloadTypeMismatch` (#84)
- Canonical corpus vectors: RegisterProject with reordered and relocated documents (same revision and bytes), a pinned ESM v2 vector, and an unsupported vector that fails closed with no artifacts. The corpus package now runs package validation (#168)
- Documentation gates: every construct the parsers accept must have a grammar production and a reference page; every relative link and anchor must resolve and every page must be reachable from navigation. Documentation-only pull requests now run these checks (#146)

## Changed

- A `file` constraint warns (`PLAY0396`): Chronicle only supports unique constraints, so declare them with `unique …`, and put other rules in validation or `require`. The constraints page now states Chronicle's actual guarantee (#223)

This release activates version 2 of the executable semantic model. It covers what version 1 could not express: which event source a state change targets, event-source context on facts, specification event sources, and command-occurrence values. A model uses version 2 only when it needs one of these; every existing model keeps its version 1 bytes. The release also executes projection variants, adds validation severities, and makes preserved comments land exactly where they were written.

## Added

- Executable semantic model version 2. It is selected automatically when a model uses a v2 construct and is otherwise unchanged at version 1 (#226, #167):
  - Typed state-change destinations: `produces … for <expr>` targets an event source without duplicating the identity into the event.
  - Event-source context on facts, which projections read the event-source identity from.
  - `for <value>` event-source assertions on `given` and `then` events, so a specification can name exact streams. For example, a unique constraint can be shown colliding between two event sources.

This release makes most of the remaining modeling language executable and keeps authored models intact through tool edits. Specification values can now be typed objects and lists, and specifications without a `when` step run. Commands can produce events conditionally and state `require` conditions. Constraints gain their lifecycle forms, and validation gains pattern matching. Canonical printing, folder expansion and MCP edits now keep comments.

## Fixed

- An `import` of a declaration from the same application no longer hides consistency diagnostics (#208)

Screenplay could describe a button but not what pressing it does. This adds the missing half of the UI story: a `behavior` - a bundle of trigger-to-action bindings - attachable at every level of the containment tree.

There is one construct behind both forms it takes. A named `behavior` is declared at the top level and attached with `uses`; an inline `on` block is the same thing without a name, attached to whatever it is written on. One record, one walker method, one printer case - anonymity is a property rather than a separate kind of node.

`trigger` still means exactly what it meant. A declared `trigger` is an application signal with a payload that a `reaction ... when` consumes; what starts an interaction is the anonymous `on` clause. The built-in kinds are reserved inside an `on` clause only, so an identifier named `click` anywhere else is still just an identifier. Declaring an application trigger named after one of them is an error, because `on <Name>` would otherwise be ambiguous.

Attachment points are complete rather than incremental: layout, screen template, dialog template, module, feature, form, screen, section, slot and table all accept the same `on`/`uses` pair through shared parse, print and walk helpers. Partial coverage would have meant explaining which half of the tree works.

Interaction constructs report `PLAY0269` - deferred from the backend ESM v1 profile - which is what every existing UI construct already reports. Blocking with `PLAY0268` would have failed compilation of any document containing a working button.

Diagnostics `PLAY0300`-`PLAY0326` cover the syntax and `PLAY0330`-`PLAY0339` the resolution, all documented in `diagnostics.md`, with a new `interactions.md` page and Monaco keywords.

An end-to-end run of the CLI over a realistic multi-file document found a bug no specification would have: `PlayFolderMerge` did not carry behaviors, so a `uses` in one file could not see a behavior declared in another. Every specification used a single source string, so the suite was green while the folder path - the one people actually use - was broken. Fixed, with a two-file specification.

2801 specifications pass.

Note for reviewers: 356 of 408 `Screenplay.Mcp` specifications fail on macOS on pristine `main` as well - `McpRoot.CheckAncestors` hits a reparse point, and `.git` is a file rather than a directory in a worktree. Confirmed by running a detached worktree of `origin/main` with no changes and getting an identical count. Unrelated to this change, but that suite currently proves nothing on a developer machine.

## Summary

Four words in the language now mean exactly one thing each: a **layout** is the application's base navigational shell, a **screen template** is a reusable shape inside it, a **dialog template** is a shape that opens over it, and a **screen** is an instance that fills one of them.

## Added

- `layout <Name>` — a new top level construct declaring the application's base navigational look: named slots, arranged the same way a template's are. Its slots keep `contributes <ContributionPoint>`, which makes the shell the natural home of an application-wide `Navigation` point.
- `layout <Name>` on a `ui profile`, exactly parallel to the existing `theme <Name>` line — at most one per profile. This is where an application states which shell it uses. Naming a layout the document does not declare is reported as a warning, the way an unknown theme already is.
- `dialog template <Name>` at module scope — a reusable shape for content that opens over the application. It declares no `fits slot`, because it occupies no slot.
- `fits slot <name>` on a screen template — names the slot of its parent the template fills. One rule for every level: a module's template fits a slot on the application layout, a feature's fits a slot the module's template declares, a slice's fits one the feature's declares.
- A `Layouts and templates` documentation page covering the four constructs and how they nest.

## Changed

- The module-scoped `layout <Name>` is now **`screen template <Name>`**. It was never a layout — it is a reusable shape that goes inside one.
- A screen names the structure it fills with **`template <Name>`** instead of `layout <Name>`.
- The arrangement tree hangs **directly off `arrangement`**; the separate `template` block inside it is gone. `arrangement freeform` likewise holds its `variant` blocks directly. This frees the word `template` to mean a screen or dialog template and nothing else.
- **Slots are declared by name in the body**, and the arrangement positions them:

  ```screenplay
  layout AppShell
    navigation contributes Navigation
    content

    arrangement flow
      row
        navigation width 240
        content grow
  ```

  A body of plain slot names, with no `arrangement`, is a complete declaration on its own. `contributes` belongs on the declaration; sizing (`width`, `height`, `grow`, `span`) belongs in the arrangement, so a slot never says two different things about itself in two places.
- Syntax types renamed to match: `LayoutSyntax` is now the application layout, `ScreenTemplateSyntax` / `DialogTemplateSyntax` are the module-scoped ones, `ModuleSyntax.Layouts` is `ModuleSyntax.ScreenTemplates` (plus `DialogTemplates`), `TemplateSyntax` and its tree are `ArrangementSyntax` / `ArrangementNodeSyntax` / `ArrangementContainerSyntax` / `ArrangementSlotSyntax` / `ArrangementOverrideSyntax` / `ArrangementContainerKind`, `LayoutArrangement` is `ArrangementMode`, and `ScreenLayoutSyntax` is `ScreenTemplateReferenceSyntax`. The matching walker methods follow the same names.

## Fixed

## Added

- **`arrangement flow`** (default) - a layout's `template` block can now nest slots under `row`/`column`/`grid` containers with sizing attributes (`width`, `height`, `grow`, `span`, `gap`), and declare `when width <compact|regular>[, height <compact|regular>]` (or `when height ...` alone) overrides that replace the tree for a given size class. A bare `template` of plain slot names still parses exactly as before - this is a purely additive language change.
- **`arrangement freeform`** - a layout can instead declare `variant width <compact|regular>, height <compact|regular>` blocks, each placing slots at pixel-precise coordinates with `place <Slot> at x,y size w,h` (either dimension may be `fill`) or hiding one with `place <Slot> hidden`. One `screen`/data/action/form contract still applies across every variant - only placement varies.
- Width/height size classes (`compact`/`regular`) are a new two-dimensional vocabulary scoped to layout arrangement, reused across both modes so phone portrait/landscape, tablet, and desktop narrow/wide fall out of the matrix without an `orientation` primitive.
- A `freeform` layout's `variant` that omits a slot another variant of the same layout places (or hides) now gets a compile-time warning.

## Notes

- **Scope decision:** arrangement is declared per-layout, not per-slot. - `authorize` carries a requirement tree rather than a flat list, so `A or B C` states which grouping it means. `AuthorizeSyntax.Policies` is replaced by `Requirement`; call `References()` for the policies alone (#68)

Both are optional — a bare `rule <Name>` is still valid for logic that stays outside the document entirely.

## Fixed

- A rule whose logic could not be expressed was left out of the document entirely, so a property with two declarative rules and three predicates read as a property with two rules — with no way for a reader to tell "nothing further constrains this" from "the rest could not be written down". (#47)

## Summary

Eight language additions delivered together, each one all the way through: grammar, compiler, printer, Monaco/VS Code language service, documentation, and the invoicing sample. The theme is that a Screenplay should be **complete and meaningful before any code exists** — several of these close gaps where the language could only point at code instead of describing behavior.

## Added

- `type <Name>` declares a composite value type — the child-record shapes events routinely carry (`lines InvoiceLine[]`). Referencable from event, command and type properties (#29)
- `pii reason "…"` / `sensitive reason "…"` in a concept body records *why* a value is personal data — purpose, lawful basis, whose subject it lives under — instead of losing it to a bare marker (#38)
- `identifier` marks the command property a runtime resolves the event source id from. At most one per command; without it a new `Uuid` is assumed (#52)
- `then error` with no reason states a rejection the specification does not name, replacing `then error ""` as the only expressible form (#46)
- `description` on a reactor and on each `on` trigger, and reactor trigger bodies are now optional — a reactor is describable before any code exists (#40)
- Queries gain a `description`, parameters sourced from the context with `from $context.…`, and a `performer` block — the query's counterpart to a command `handler`, as a `file` reference or an inline `csharp`/`sql` block (#53)
- `CommandContext` and `QueryContext` in `Cratis.Screenplay.Contexts` establish what a command handler and a query performer are given — the command or arguments, `TenantId`, `CausedBy`, `Causation` and when it occurred (#54, #55)
- `sql` as an inline code block language
- Documentation pages for composite types and for the command and query context, plus a declarative-first section in the grammar stating that a document must be expressible — and meaningful — with zero `file` references

## Changed

- `$context.` paths are validated against the members of `CommandContext`/`QueryContext` — `command`, `arguments`, `tenant`, `causedBy`, `causation`, `occurred`, `identity` — and an unknown path is reported
- Property and query-parameter type references resolve against the primitives, declared concepts, declared types and imports; a reference to something the document never declares is reported. Query return types name read models and are not checked
- Concept and type names share one namespace, so declaring both is an error
- `ConceptSyntax.Attributes` is now `IEnumerable<ConceptAttributeSyntax>` (name plus optional reason); `ConceptSyntax.AttributeNames` gives the previous string sequence
- `SpecificationErrorSyntax.Name` is nullable — `null` is a rejection with no named reason
- The Monaco language service and the VS Code extension know every new construct: keywords, completions, hover, embedded SQL highlighting, and diagnostics matching the compiler

The escape already existed in projections and now works for property lines, property mappings, enumeration values and projection `from` mappings everywhere. (#27)

## Fixed

- Stage's semantic runtime now has Chronicle reject its append atomically when another writer appended to the event log after Stage captured the tail, including the first append to an empty log. Before, the append succeeded and the divergence was only detected on the next command. The runtime faults with "the event-log tail changed outside this session", and nothing is appended.

This closes the external-append race. It does not detect another writer revising or replacing existing events in place.

A body the model references that is missing, refused by the loader, or changed since compilation fails with `STAGE-ESM-020`, which names the requirement and the loader's reason (`PLAY0430`–`PLAY0434`), and no artifacts are produced.

## Changed

Stage never emits a policy with a substituted time or a predicate that silently denies.

## Fixed

- An unsupported authorization result is no longer replaced by a contract rejection when the command payload fails to bind.

## Added

- The opt-in semantic Stage engine (`Stage__Runtime__Engine=semantic`) can start on a Chronicle event log that already holds events. It rebuilds its semantic world only when that can be done exactly: every projection is mirrored exactly and has caught up with its own events without failed partitions, every logged event converts back exactly, and the history satisfies the model's constraints. Otherwise it refuses with a specific `Unsupported(World)` status. (part of #23)

## Changed

- The semantic engine reports `loading` while it rebuilds, and refuses requests until it is ready. After any append by another client it stops serving requests rather than drift from the log. (part of #23)
- A rebuild is refused for event contracts with date-time or decimal properties, because Chronicle's storage changes those values (offsets, precision). It is also refused for null optional values, non-text destinations, a `causedBy` name that changed over time, and duplicate tags. The bundled sandbox container resets its kernel on restart, so rebuilding applies when the host runs against an external or persistent Chronicle. (part of #23)

## Added

- A render profile can carry the model's `.strings` catalog. Generated validators then resolve `$strings.<key>` rule and requirement messages for the request's UI culture, falling back through its parent cultures to the default locale. A screen's own \`table\` and \`summary\` widgets never received the API route that lets them read real data. Not because a query was missing - because the property naming the read model didn't match what the route-resolution pass looks for.

## The mismatch

A running Stage attaches an element's route (\`StageSceneRoutes.WithRoutes\`) by matching a registered endpoint against the modeled artifact's type name, read from one specific property: \`SceneSynthesizer.TypeNameProperty\` (\`"typeName"\`). \`SceneSynthesizer\` itself - which builds the *default* scene when a document declares no screens - writes that property correctly. \`ScreenDirectiveConverter\`, which converts a document's *own* \`table\` and \`summary\` directives, wrote the read model's name under \`"target"\` instead.

The resolution pass fails silently: an element missing the property it looks for is just returned unchanged, with no route and no error. A table naming its read model under the wrong key renders exactly as well as one naming it correctly - same headers, same columns - and the two are indistinguishable until something tries to read data through it. Which is exactly what \`InvoiceList\` in \`Samples/Billing\` looked like: a fully modeled table, showing \`No query is exposed for InvoiceSummary yet\` for a read model with a query right above it in the same file.

## The fix

Both converters now write \`SceneElementProperties.TypeName\` - the same constant, moved out of \`Stage.Api\` (which \`Contracts\` cannot see without a circular project reference) into \`Contracts.Scene\`, where the converters already live. \`SceneSynthesizer.TypeNameProperty\` becomes an alias to it, so nothing that already referenced it has to change.

## Verification

A new specification proves both converters carry the read model under the property a route actually resolves against - the property name itself is now something a specification can hold accountable, rather than an assumption two files have to keep agreeing on by hand.

Beyond that, verified against a running sandbox rather than only in-process: rebuilt the \`cratis/stage\` image with this change, ran \`cratis run\` against \`Samples/Billing\`, registered an invoice through the real command route, and watched the browser go from \`No query is exposed\` to a table showing that invoice's number and amount, fetched through the route this fix attaches.

1675 backend specifications pass, plus the frontend's 8 (its own \`route\`-driven behavior was already correct and already specified; this fix is entirely on the side that failed to supply one).

Completes the chain Screenplay 4.17.0 and Scene 4.0.0 built: a `.play` document says `on click / execute CancelInvoice`, and clicking the rendered button posts that command to the route this Stage registered for it.

## Translation

`BehaviorConverter`, `InteractionActionConverter` and `BehaviorAttachments` carry a compiled document's interactions into the Scene model. A `uses` naming a behavior the document does not declare is reported as a finding and dropped, never substituted with an empty behavior.

Module and feature attachments have no node of their own in the Scene model, so they fold onto the screens beneath them, outermost first - the order the engine runs them in, and what lets a module gate everything below it without every screen cooperating.

## The running frontend

An element already carried the route it is backed by, which is enough for an element that *is* a command. An interaction is not: it names a command that may live anywhere in the model, attached to a button that knows nothing about it. `/stage/routes` serves that lookup, resolved from the same endpoint set the elements use, so an interaction and an action cannot disagree about where the same command lives.

A command this Stage does not serve is reported rather than guessed at - a guessed URL turns a modelling mistake into a 404 long after the cause.

Arc answers a rejected command with 200 and the reasons, so the status alone does not say whether it worked. The dispatcher reads the body, which is what makes a document's own `on failure` branch mean what it says instead of firing only on transport failures.

## Samples

`Samples/Billing` is a complete application - two modules, four features, eight slices, fourteen files - covering 112 of the language's constructs, including both sub-languages, both arrangement kinds and inline C# in each of the four places it is allowed. It is compiled by the test run, asserting zero errors, zero warnings and zero translation findings, so it cannot rot into something that no longer compiles while being read as documentation.

It found two defects that 1573 existing specifications missed, both fixed here:

- `target size expanded` - valid Screenplay, used in Screenplay's own documentation - **crashed** the translation, because a target's assumed size was parsed against the two-axis arrangement matrix, which has no such value.
- Behaviors written inside a filled template slot were **dropped without a word**, because the conversion only read a screen's top-level directives. Nobody writes an interaction at the top of a templated screen; they write it next to the thing it acts on, which is exactly what no unit specification did.

---

**Multi-target builds — the open question in #39, answered: one invocation produces one plan per target, never a build per target.**

Targets come out of a single compile of a single `.play` source set, so planning them together is the only way they are guaranteed to describe the same application; a build per target compiles the same source once per target and can only compare outcomes afterwards, if at all. It is also what makes "this template is unplaceable on the phone but fine on the web" answerable at all, and what lets a build fail once, coherently, with every target's findings in hand. Planning together does not force emitting together — `Targets` is a list and each entry is independently emittable, so shipping one target now and another later is a filter over the plan. The split belongs at emission, where the artifacts genuinely differ, not back at compilation, where they do not. The reasoning is stated on `ApplicationRenderPlan` itself, and `RenderPlanner` deliberately exposes no single-target entry point.

**On #39's third bullet — build diagnostics through Screenplay's channel.** Not done, and deliberately. `EventModelLoader` throws `InvalidEventModel` before any of this runs when the *compilation* has errors, so a plan is always built on a diagnostic-clean tree. What a plan finds is a different class: valid source that turns out to be under-specified for one concrete target. It belongs to a target rather than to a span of source text, which is what Screenplay's diagnostic channel describes — so it lives on the returned plan. Piping these back would be its own piece of work and would need a target-attributed diagnostic first.

**Documented gaps.** A catalog carries package names and the names of what each package contributes, never structures — so a shell provided by a blueprint package is named in the plan (`LayoutName`) and carries no structure, and its arrangements and template placements are not part of that plan. Emission itself is out of scope: a plan is the resolved input an emitter consumes.

## Context

`Screen`/`Layout`/`ScreenTemplate`/`DialogTemplate`/`Form`/`Contribution` translate close to directly. The shape gaps that remain are documented inline rather than silently worked around:

- `ui profile`'s `theme` and `layout` references, a form's `on submit navigate to`, and a slot's `contributes` have no field on the corresponding Scene types yet - all called out as deliberate, documented gaps rather than silently dropped.
- A screen with no `template` directive (a Level 1 "intent" screen, where Studio generates the component) fills the layout's `content` slot directly and names no template - which is exactly what `Screen.ScreenTemplate` documents `null` to mean. Nothing is synthesized for it.
- A document that declares no `layout` at all gets one synthesized shell for the whole application, never one per screen.

Every screen directive (`data`, `action`, `navigate`, `section`, `title`, `table`, `summary`, `code`) converts to one `ExternalComponent` named `core:<kind>`, with its own fields folded into the open `properties` bag. This is deliberately mechanical rather than a bespoke `SceneElement` subtype per widget - the `core:*` components don't need to exist in `Scene.React` yet for the translated model to be correct; rendering them is a separate, later concern.

### New template: `cratis-aspire`

```bash
dotnet new cratis-aspire -n MyApp

Generates a three-project solution:

| Project | Role |
|---|---|
| `MyApp/` | Cratis Arc + Chronicle web app (same vertical-slice structure as `cratis`) |

### Composition (AppHost)

Wires Chronicle as an Aspire resource using `Cratis.Chronicle.Aspire` (the forthcoming package from Chronicle#2798):

var chronicle = builder.AddCratisChronicle();

    .WithReference(chronicle)
    .WaitFor(chronicle);
```

### Infrastructure (ServiceDefaults)

Provides `AddServiceDefaults()` and `MapDefaultEndpoints()` extensions consumed by the main app — covering OTLP export, metrics/tracing instrumentation, HTTP resilience, and service discovery. Chronicle and MongoDB connection strings are omitted from `appsettings.json`; Aspire injects them at runtime.

- Three GUIDs generated for the solution file (`ProjectGuid`, `CompositionGuid`, `InfrastructureGuid`)
- `sourceName: CratisAspire` handles directory, file, and namespace renaming across all three projects

## Summary

An invitation link asked the person to pick an identity provider twice. The first
choice signed them in and returned them to a second, identical selection page;
only the pass after that completed the invitation and reached the application.

A deployment that declares a frontend is routed with a catch-all covering every
path, and that route carries the default `RequireAuthenticatedUser` policy. It
matched `/invite/{token}` and `/register` too, so authorization refused both
before the middleware that owns each flow ever ran. Nothing was staged and no
pending-invitation cookie was set, so the sign-in that followed carried no
capability binding and the invitation could not complete — until a later pass,
by which time the first one had finally planted the cookie it needed.

## Fixed

- An invitation link no longer asks for an identity provider a second time after signing in, and completes on the first attempt.
- `/invite` and `/register` are answered by the invitation and registration flows in every deployment, instead of being redirected to provider selection wherever a catch-all route covers them.

## Fixed

- Accepting an invitation no longer shows a second provider-selection page: the invitation now completes on the provider sign-in callback itself, so it no longer depends on the browser presenting the fresh session cookie on the follow-up request.
- After a completed invitation, the sign-in redirects straight to the lobby for a create-organization invitation and to the original return URL for a tenant-issued one; a failed exchange on the callback answers with the same page or redirect the post-login exchange produces.
- A browser replaying the invitation URL or a stale pending-invitation cookie after completion is recognized as already answered instead of being offered provider selection again or re-running the exchange.

## Fixed

- Accepting an invitation no longer loops back to provider selection after a successful sign-in: the completion gate now accepts any session that was signed in while the invitation was pending — the person's deliberate choice for it — and only a session that predates the invitation is taken through provider selection. This repairs the regression 2.17.2 introduced for deployments where the challenge's capability binding does not survive the provider round trip.

## Fixed

- An invitation is now completed only with the identity that authenticated for that invitation. A session the browser was already carrying — from an earlier sign-in, possibly with a different provider — no longer completes a pending invitation, so an organization can no longer be bound permanently to an account the person did not choose for it.
- A caller who is already signed in and opens an invitation link is now always shown the invitation provider-selection page, including where only a single identity provider is configured, and the invitation completes with the identity that comes back from the provider they pick.
- A pending invitation is left in place when it cannot yet be completed, so it stays valid for the lifetime of the `.cratis-invite` cookie instead of being consumed by the wrong session.
- Invite-token re-validation at the post-login exchange is unchanged: a forged, expired, or otherwise invalid capability is still refused with `invitation-invalid.html` / `invitation-expired.html` and cleared from the browser before anything else is decided.

## Fixed

- Microsoft sign-ins and credential links through a multi-tenant authority (`common`, `organizations`, `consumers`) no longer fail issuer validation (IDX10205) — the issuer is validated against the tenant the token itself names, for both organizational and personal accounts.
- Sign-ins and credential links are now attributed to the identity provider that was actually challenged, instead of falling back to the meaningless `AuthenticationTypes.Federation` some providers leave as the principal's authentication type.

## Summary

Every OIDC handshake (Microsoft, Google) failed with "Correlation failed" and looped back to provider selection, because the handler's default `form_post` response mode returns the authorization code in a cross-site POST — which browsers never attach the `SameSite=Lax` correlation cookie to. This surfaced hardest in the credential-link flow (Cratis/StudioIssues#104), where the failure additionally landed on the sign-in selection page, offering to replace the very session the link was preserving. The link flow is now also embeddable in the product's modal iframe, with the provider leg in its own top-level window.
